issues.subcategory: Contradictory SESOI / equivalence bound values
issues.description: The analytic plan first states the smallest effect size of interest is δ = .27, but in the detailed justification the authors state they set the equivalence region to δ = .11. These two values are used to define the equivalence interval that is central to every confirmatory test of the null-result hypotheses (gambling and substances). A factor-of-2.5 discrepancy in the equivalence bound directly determines whether equivalence is declared, so this contradiction makes the primary analyses uninterpretable as written.
issues.quote: with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent operational definition of moral incongruence
issues.description: Moral incongruence is defined throughout the abstract, introduction, and hypotheses as the interaction of moral disapproval and behavioral FREQUENCY. However, in 'The Present Study' the central operationalization is described as the interaction of moral disapproval with 'severity of consequences,' a different construct. Because moral incongruence is the focal predictor, this inconsistency leaves the actual tested model ambiguous and could change the meaning of every reported effect.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction over who completes problematic-use measures
issues.description: The Measures section states problematic-use items are only completed by those who endorse past-year use, but the Data Screening section states all participants complete problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures regardless of engagement. These two procedures yield very different analytic samples (the power table assumes user-only subsets), and the contradiction affects sample sizes, the interaction term, and interpretation of every model.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.subcategory: Inference of uniqueness from significant-vs-nonsignificant comparison
issues.description: The core claim—that moral incongruence is 'unique' to sexual behavior—rests on finding a significant interaction for pornography and equivalence/non-significance for other behaviors in SEPARATE models. Concluding that domains differ because one effect is significant and another is not is a well-known statistical fallacy; uniqueness requires a formal test of the difference between interaction coefficients across domains (e.g., a behavior-type three-way interaction), which is never specified. The equivalence tests partially mitigate but do not establish a difference.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: Averaging items measured on incompatible response scales
issues.description: The substance/behavior problematic-use score averages three items scored 0–5 with two items scored on a 0/3/6 scale. Averaging items with different numbers of categories and different maxima without rescaling distorts the composite, gives the 0/3/6 items disproportionate weight, and is psychometrically unjustified, undermurdering the validity of the primary outcome for substances.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: Criterion contamination between predictor and outcome
issues.description: The frequency predictor and the problematic-use outcome share content and method variance: the NIDA-ASSIST 'problematic use' items are themselves frequency-of-symptom questions ('how often have you had a strong desire or urge', scored 0=never to 5=more than once per day, the same scale as the frequency predictor). Higher behavioral frequency mechanically inflates urge/consequence frequency, which can spuriously produce or distort the frequency×disapproval interaction.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use (“In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?”

issues.subcategory: Non-equivalent outcome measures across compared domains
issues.description: The uniqueness comparison hinges on parallel measurement, yet the primary outcomes differ by domain: pornography uses the Brief Pornography Screen, gambling uses the PGSI, and substances use an unvalidated averaged NIDA-ASSIST composite. Different, differentially validated instruments with different scaling, time frames, and item content confound any cross-domain comparison of interaction magnitudes.
issues.quote: with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.subcategory: Oversample undermines representativeness for gambling (and substances)
issues.description: The combined N≈4,000 includes a 1,500-person oversample of past-year sports bettors. The manuscript repeatedly calls the sample 'nationally representative' and the power table pools the oversample into gambling analyses (effective N = 3,325) without describing any weighting. The gambling subsample is therefore strongly non-representative, and sports bettors also likely differ in substance use, so substance estimates based on the full 4,000 are also biased. Representativeness is overclaimed.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: Unrealistic assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The authors assert there will be essentially no missingness and no need to remove cases, citing YouGov proprietary standards, and provide no plan for handling missing responses, careless responding, or partial completion. This assumption is implausible for a 4,000-person multi-domain survey and leaves the analysis with no specified missing-data strategy, threatening replicability and validity.
issues.quote: Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: Data-dependent redefinition of the equivalence region
issues.description: The contingency plan redefines the equivalence bound using the lower 95% CI limit of the pornography interaction estimated from the same dataset. Setting the SESOI from observed in-sample effects is circular and data-dependent, converting an a priori equivalence test into a post hoc comparison whose properties (error rates) are no longer controlled. This is an undisclosed-degrees-of-freedom problem even though it is described.
issues.quote: we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent number of analyses / substance list
issues.description: The text states 8 moderation analyses for 8 'target behaviors/variables,' but Table 1 lists only 7 outcomes (alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription, illicit, pornography, gambling). The count of 8 appears to come from treating 'tobacco' and 'non-tobacco nicotine' as separate substances in the averaging text, yet the actual survey item combines all tobacco/nicotine products into a single question. The number of analyses and the substance taxonomy are therefore internally inconsistent.
issues.quote: averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent frequency response-scale coding
issues.description: Frequency scales are described inconsistently: substance frequency as 0 (never) to 5, but pornography and gambling frequency as 1 (never) to 6. The supplemental materials code all of these as 0 (never) to 5. These discrepancies affect centering, the interaction term, and reproducibility of the analyses.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: Mismatched reference time frames across measures
issues.description: The predictor (frequency) refers to the past 12 months, the NIDA-ASSIST problematic-use items to the past 3 months, the Brief Pornography Screen to the past 6 months, and the PGSI to the past 12 months, while moral disapproval has no time frame. Combining variables with differing temporal windows in a single moderation model can attenuate or distort the frequency×disapproval interaction and complicates interpretation.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, “In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?”

issues.subcategory: Uncorrected multiple comparisons in primary tests
issues.description: Eight primary moderation analyses (plus direct-effect tests and equivalence tests) are planned, but correction for multiple comparisons is specified only for the bivariate correlations (Holm), not for the focal interaction tests. With multiple confirmatory tests and a pre-stated expectation of one positive and several null results, the absence of an error-rate control for the primary analyses inflates the risk of spurious conclusions.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: Single-item moral disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval—a key construct entering every interaction—is measured with a single item per behavior, providing no internal-consistency estimate and limited content coverage of a multidimensional construct. Single-item predictors with unknown reliability attenuate and bias interaction estimates, which is especially consequential for equivalence tests designed to detect small effects.
issues.quote: we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: Pornography frequency item narrower than definition
issues.description: The pornography definition is broad (films, clips, pictures, internet/magazine/book/TV), but the frequency item assesses only 'Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner).' Restricting the frequency measure to solitary use creates a mismatch between the operationalization and the construct and may misclassify users, affecting the interaction with disapproval.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: Alcohol operationalization departs from validated screen
issues.description: The authors discard the validated binge-quantity anchoring of the NIDA Quick Screen and instead assess general alcohol frequency without specifying quantity. This changes what the alcohol exposure variable measures (any drinking vs. risky drinking), reducing comparability with prior validation and with the problem-use criterion, and potentially weakening detection of meaningful incongruence effects.
issues.quote: for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: Confirmation-oriented framing of hypotheses
issues.description: The stated aim is to 'demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique,' and the authors describe a disconfirming outcome as 'especially unlikely.' Framing a registered confirmatory study around demonstrating a desired conclusion (rather than neutrally testing it) signals motivated reasoning and increases the risk that flexible decisions (e.g., SESOI choice, equivalence-region switching) are deployed to favor the preferred result.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Vague, undisclosed robustness procedures
issues.description: Handling of assumption violations is left open-ended ('supplemental analyses... as appropriate'), without specifying which alternative estimators, thresholds for 'substantial' violation, or decision rules will be used. This leaves undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom in a Registered Report, where such contingencies should be fully pre-specified.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of ICD-11 caveat
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly notes the ICD-11 states moral distress is 'not sufficient' for CSBD (an exclusionary safeguard), yet here frames it as a decision 'to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration,' which inverts the meaning. The Public Significance Statement compounds this by implying inclusion. This conceptual slippage misrepresents the diagnostic rationale the study claims to support.
issues.quote: consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD

issues.subcategory: Causal language from cross-sectional/correlational evidence
issues.description: The Public Significance Statement asserts moral-values violation is a 'leading contributor' to self-reported sexual addiction. The cited evidence is cross-sectional/correlational, and the present design is explicitly cross-sectional (as acknowledged in Limitations). Causal/contributory language overstates what the data can support.
issues.quote: a body of research clearly indicates that distress over sexual behaviors that violates personal morality is a leading contributor to self-reported feelings of sexual addiction and compulsivity.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent reported effect-size values for cited studies
issues.description: The same Grubbs, Lee et al. (2020) small effect is reported with Cohen's d = .22 in one sentence and d = .25 in another; similarly the SESOI is described as f2 = .015 in the power section but f2 = .016 in the effect-size review. These inconsistencies in the numbers used to justify the equivalence region and power analyses undermine confidence in the quantitative justification.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: Binary gender coding excludes non-binary participants
issues.description: Gender is operationalized as binary (1 = male, 0 = not-male) and the alcohol items branch only on MAN/WOMAN. This collapses or omits non-binary respondents, mismatches the claim of population representativeness, and may misassign the sex-specific binge-drinking thresholds.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: Incomplete/garbled methods sentence
issues.description: The description of the power analyses contains an incomplete clause ('a series of estimated achieved power based.'), leaving unclear what the estimated achieved power analyses were based on. This is a reporting gap in a section central to evaluating whether the equivalence tests are adequately powered.
issues.quote: a series of estimated achieved power based.

issues.subcategory: Supplemental binge-drinking item label inconsistency
issues.description: The supplemental male-version alcohol item asks about 'more than 5 drinks' in the prompt but labels the response row 'More than four drinks,' identical to the female version. This labeling error could cause miscoding of the sex-specific binge item.
issues.quote: In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?
